rule: Code outside a method body: the caller is its location. Field/val initializer → `Type#field`; C# property accessor → `Type#Prop` (get) / `Type#Prop=` (set); Ruby setter → `Type#x=`; `static {}` block → `Type#<clinit>`. Non-lazy initializers also get an `implicit` edge from `<clinit>`/`<init>`; lazy ones do not. | `implicit`: an execution edge the language runs without a written call — `Type#<clinit>` → `Type#field` (static initializer), `Type#<init>` → `Type#field` (instance field initializer). Line = the field's line. | module = the file's path below the scan root without extension and trailing `/index` (`src/chat` for src/chat/index.ts; basenames collide across directories): `src/app.f`, `src/app.C#m`, `#<init>`/`#<clinit>`/`#field` as in Java. | Call on a receiver of **unknown type**: `recv.member`, using the LAST receiver segment (`self.client.get()` → `client.get`; `a.b.c()` → `b.c`).
notes: Static field `items` and instance field `count` are field initializers: caller `Type#field`, plus an implicit edge from `<clinit>` (static) / `<init>` (instance) on the field's line. The JS note says `#<init>`/`#<clinit>`/`#field` work 'as in Java'. The implicit edges' confidence is high: SPEC gives no tier for implicit edges; both endpoints are defined in the scan, which is the high tier. The `static {}` block's code has caller `Registry#<clinit>`. `Registry.items` has no declared type -> `items.push` (last receiver segment), low. Every field initializer in this case contains a call, so the open question of literal-only initializers does not arise.
